title: Foundations of Geographic Thought
description: Explore the history of geographic thought and major theories.
objectives: Trace the history of geography as a discipline
Apply geographic theories to real cases

lessons.title: History of Geography
lessons.content: Geography as a systematic discipline dates to ancient Greece.
examples: Eratosthenes (276–194 BCE): first to calculate Earth's circumference accurately — was off by only ~2%
Ibn Battuta (1304–1368): greatest pre-modern traveler; 120,000 km across Africa, Middle East, Asia, Europe
Humboldt and Ritter (19th c.): founded modern systematic geography
Mackinder's Heartland Theory (1904): whoever controls central Eurasia controls the world

lessons.title: Environmental Determinism vs. Possibilism
lessons.content: Two contrasting views on how geography affects human society.
examples: Determinism: climate and geography determine culture and economic development (now discredited as often used to justify racism)
Possibilism: geography creates constraints and opportunities, but human agency determines outcomes
Example: Netherlands — coastal lowlands are a disadvantage, but the Dutch built the world's most advanced flood management system

title: Geomorphology — Earth's Landforms
description: Study the processes that create and shape Earth's landforms.
objectives: Explain tectonic forces that build landforms
Describe gradational forces that erode landforms

lessons.title: Tectonic and Volcanic Landforms
lessons.content: Internal Earth forces create dramatic landforms.
examples: Fold mountains: Himalayas, Alps — plates collide, crust crumples upward
Rift valleys: East African Rift — plates pull apart; eventually will flood, creating new ocean
Volcanic island chains: Hawaii — hotspot in the mantle burns through moving plate, creating island chain

lessons.title: Coastal Geography
lessons.content: Coastlines are among Earth's most dynamic landforms.
examples: Beaches: wave deposition; beach drift moves sand along the coast
Sea caves, arches, stacks: wave erosion carved into cliffs
Coral reefs: biogenic (built by living organisms); require warm, clear, shallow water
Mangroves: tropical coastal forests that protect coastlines and serve as fish nurseries

title: Climatology — Advanced
description: Advanced study of climate systems, Koppen classification, and climate change projections.
objectives: Apply the Koppen climate classification system
Explain ENSO (El Niño/La Niña) and other oscillations

lessons.title: Koppen Climate Classification
lessons.content: The Koppen system classifies climates into five major groups based on temperature and precipitation.
examples: A (tropical): hot all year, high rainfall — Amazon, Congo, Southeast Asia
B (dry): precipitation < evapotranspiration — Sahara, Gobi, Atacama
C (temperate): mild winters — most of Europe, eastern US, China coast
D (continental): cold winters — interior North America, Russia
E (polar): average temperature below 10°C even in warmest month — Greenland, Antarctica

lessons.title: ENSO and Climate Variability
lessons.content: El Niño Southern Oscillation is the world's most powerful year-to-year climate driver.
examples: El Niño: warm water in central Pacific → drought in Australia/Southeast Asia, flooding in South America, warmer U.S. winters
La Niña: opposite pattern
ENSO affects 2+ billion people's food and water security annually
Record strong El Niño (2015–16): contributed to global temperature record

title: Political Geography — Nation-States and Boundaries
description: Analyze political geography — how power is organized in space.

lessons.title: States and Nations
lessons.content: 'State' (political territory) and 'nation' (shared identity) are often confused but distinct.
examples: Nation-state: state where political and national boundaries align (Japan, Iceland)
Multinational state: state with multiple nations (Nigeria: 250+ ethnic groups; India: 2,000+ ethnic groups)
Stateless nations: Kurds (~40 million people; no state of their own), Palestinians, Catalans

lessons.title: Boundaries
lessons.content: Boundaries organize political space; their location and type matters enormously.
examples: Natural boundaries: rivers (Rhine, Rio Grande), mountain ranges (Pyrenees, Himalayas)
Geometric boundaries: straight lines — often colonial relics (Africa, Middle East, American West)
Relic boundaries: former boundaries that still influence culture (old Iron Curtain, former East/West Germany divisions)

title: Population Geography — Advanced
description: Advanced study of population geography — distribution, growth, and demographic theory.

lessons.title: Demographic Transition Model
lessons.content: The DTM describes how birth and death rates change as societies develop.
examples: Stage 1: high birth and death rates — stable, low population (pre-industrial)
Stage 2: death rates fall, birth rates still high — rapid population growth (early industrial)
Stage 3: birth rates begin to fall — growth slows (industrializing)
Stage 4: low birth and death rates — stable or slow growth (developed)
Stage 5 (proposed): birth rates below death rates — population shrinks (Japan, Germany)

lessons.title: Population Pyramids
lessons.content: Population pyramids show the age-sex structure of a population.
examples: Wide base: young, growing population (Nigeria, Afghanistan)
Narrow base: aging population (Japan, Italy, Germany)
Bulge: baby boom generation moving through middle age (U.S., Europe)
Policy implications: wide base → need for schools and jobs; narrow base → need for elder care and immigration

title: Economic Geography — Development and Trade
description: Advanced study of economic geography — development models and global trade patterns.

lessons.title: Development Models
lessons.content: Theorists have proposed models to explain why some countries are rich and others poor.
examples: Rostow's Stages (1960): traditional → preconditions → takeoff → drive to maturity → mass consumption
Critique: Rostow assumed all countries would follow Western path; ignores colonial history
Wallerstein's World Systems Theory: 'core' (rich) countries exploit 'periphery' (poor) through trade — inequality is structural

lessons.title: Global Trade Patterns
lessons.content: Global trade is geographically concentrated and reflects power relationships.
examples: BRICS (Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa): emerging economic powers challenging Western dominance
Global value chains: components made in many countries; China assembles iPhones but captures only ~$8 of $1,000 iPhone value
Trade wars: U.S.-China tariffs reshaped supply chains — companies moving to Vietnam, India, Mexico

title: Urban Geography — Advanced
description: Advanced study of urban systems, urban structure, and urban challenges.
objectives: Apply urban structure models (Burgess, Hoyt, Harris-Ullman)

lessons.title: Urban Structure Models
lessons.content: Geographers have developed models to explain urban land use patterns.
examples: Burgess Concentric Ring Model (1925): CBD → factory zone → working-class housing → middle-class → commuters
Hoyt Sector Model (1939): cities grow in wedge-shaped sectors along transportation routes
Harris-Ullman Multiple Nuclei Model (1945): cities have multiple centers (e.g., different ethnic neighborhoods)

lessons.title: Gentrification and Planning
lessons.content: Gentrification transforms urban neighborhoods — with benefits and costs.
examples: Gentrification: investment in previously disinvested neighborhood → rising property values → displacement of long-term residents
Brooklyn (NYC), Hackney (London), Kreuzberg (Berlin): transformed in 20 years
Inclusive planning: community land trusts, affordable housing mandates, anti-displacement policies

title: Geographic Hazards and Risk
description: Analyze the geographic dimensions of natural and human-made hazards.

lessons.title: Hazard, Risk, and Vulnerability
lessons.content: The same hazard creates very different risks depending on vulnerability.
examples: Hazard: earthquake. Risk = hazard × exposure × vulnerability
Chile vs. Haiti 2010 earthquake: both ~7.0 magnitude; Chile (wealthy, strict building codes, preparedness): ~500 deaths; Haiti (poor, weak infrastructure): 200,000+ deaths
Vulnerability: physical (building quality), social (inequality, governance), economic (insurance, reserves)

lessons.title: Disaster Risk Reduction
lessons.content: Investment in DRR before disasters saves lives and money.
examples: Bangladesh cyclone early warning: deaths reduced from 500,000 (1970) to <10,000 (2007) with same-intensity storms
Sendai Framework (2015): global plan to reduce disaster risk
Every $1 spent on DRR saves $4–7 in disaster response

title: Geography of Health
description: Apply geographic analysis to understand global patterns of health and disease.
objectives: Explain geographic factors affecting health outcomes

lessons.title: Disease Geography
lessons.content: Disease distribution follows geographic patterns related to climate, poverty, and infrastructure.
examples: Malaria: tropical belt between 30°N and 30°S; endemic in 87 countries
COVID-19 spread: followed airline routes and urban density, then income patterns (richer countries could vaccinate faster)
Geography of NCDs: non-communicable diseases (heart disease, diabetes, cancer) are rising fastest in middle-income countries

title: Applied Geography — Problem Solving
description: Apply geographic tools and thinking to solve real-world problems.
objectives: Use geographic methods to analyze a local issue

lessons.title: Applied Geography Projects
lessons.content: Geography provides powerful tools for real-world problem-solving.
examples: Crime mapping: police use GIS to identify hotspots and allocate resources
Epidemiology: trace disease sources geographically (John Snow mapped 1854 cholera outbreak to a water pump)
Urban heat islands: map temperature variations in cities to guide tree planting and cool roof programs
Food desert mapping: identify areas without grocery stores to prioritize new markets or transport routes
